    #161536. Breaking: Does culture change people’s personalities?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2826 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Does culture change people’s personalities?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, personality is often misunderstood.
    • For instance, people tend to think they are way more unpredictable and complex than they are according to others, to the point of mistakenly assuming that their “personality changes from one situation to the next”.
    • In a recent development, and yet, even if humans are predictable, that doesn’t mean that they are rigid or unable to flex according to the demands of the situation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, personality is often misunderstood. For instance, people tend to think they are way more unpredictable and complex than they are according to others, to the point of mistakenly assuming that their “personality changes from one situation to the next”. In fact, everybody has a preferred pattern of reactions to different situations, and if you hang out with people long enough you will have no trouble predicting how they are likely to act in any given situation, or indeed understanding what makes them tick. And yet, even if humans are predictable, that doesn’t mean that they are rigid or unable to flex according to the demands of the situation. One of the earliest findings in psychology is that behavior is always a function of both the person and the situation, which means that in order to predict how people will act you must take into account not just who they are but also what the situational requirements are. Micro vs. Macro At the micro-level, this explains why personality may be “suppressed” or inhibited in strong situations, that is contexts where there is a great deal of pressure to behave in a specific way or form: from a church (quiet, respectful, pensative) to a nightclub (loud, extraverted, energetic), to a lecture (focused, pensative, attentive), to a soccer game (depending on where you are, anywhere from excited and energized to aggressive and stressed). That is not to say that people stop being who they are when they are required to inhibit their personality; but rather, that personality becomes a weaker predictor of behavior when the strength of the situation temporarily eclipses it. At the macro-level, this begs the question of how much our personality may change when we make substantial long-term changes in our chosen environments or contexts. Most notably, people changing jobs or employers will often switch from one organizational culture to another; and people switching cities or countries will also be faced with different cultural demands to adapt or adjust their behaviors. Let me use myself as an example: moving from Argentina to Britain first, then from Britain to the US, required shaping my main adaptations to meet the cultural demands of each environment: I first learned to become less excitable, emotional, and direct (all of which work far less in Britain than Argentina), and then learned to suppress the sarcasm, nuances and indirectness in my communication (as these are less effective in the US than Britain). But, what does the research show about how culture, either at the societal or organizational level, impacts people’s behavior? And can this impact be significant or consequential enough to translate into actual personality changes? Adaptations Let’s start with the second question, which is actually simpler. Since personality can mostly be understood as “what you typically or habitually do,” enduring changes to how you behave—new adaptations—will indeed be perceived as personality changes. So, for instance, after living in NYC for over a decade the fast-paced nature of the city can make you more impatient, to a point that may not make you stand out in NYC (where type-A impatience is the norm) but will certainly stand out if you transfer that impactience to slower tempo cultures. As the famous line suggests, “The problem with city people in the countryside is that they expect even nature to meet deadlines.” Note, however, that city people often come from the countryside in the first place, but unless they adapt to their new fast environments and adopt the appropriate speed, they will not last very long. As for the first question, there’s plenty of research evidence—especially recent scientific papers—showing that while the essence of personality may remain largely unchanged even after people switch cultures, there are still logical changes to their personality at the more granular level, which correspond to the adaptational requirements of their adoptive cultures. In a way, we could say that our personality evolves when we go outside our comfort zone and challenge ourselves with new contexts that require new adaptations and broadening the behavioral repertoire in our tool kit. For example, a recent longitudinal study comparing 300 Japanese students studying in the United States with 108 students who remained in Japan found that international experiences were associated with changes in personality-related behaviors, particularly greater openness to new experiences and more socially adaptive behavior. Interestingly, the researchers also found that students who chose to study abroad already differed from those who stayed home, suggesting that personality not only influences how we adapt to new environments, but also which environments we choose to enter in the first place. Likewise, a recent meta-analysis examining 25 studies, comprising 40 samples and over 5,700 participants, found that living and studying abroad was associated with measurable personality changes, including increased openness to experience, greater self-confidence and agency, and lower levels of neuroticism (that is, greater emotional stability). Although the effects were generally small, the findings suggest that personality is not simply something we carry with us wherever we go, but also something that is shaped by the environments and cultures we inhabit. In another longitudinal study tracking 180 British university students, some of whom spent a year abroad across 32 different destinations, those living overseas became somewhat more agreeable, curious, and less anxious than their peers who remained at home. Interestingly, although the overall personality changes were relatively small, the researchers found that people’s everyday behavioral tendencies predicted longer-term personality change, suggesting that adapting how we behave in unfamiliar environments may eventually influence who we become. Perhaps even more intriguingly, a series of four studies examining Spanish-English bilinguals found that people’s reported personality characteristics varied depending on the language they were using. Specifically, participants tended to report higher levels of extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness when responding in English rather than Spanish, consistent with the cultural norms associated with each language. This suggests that our personality is not always expressed in the same way across situations, and that simply switching languages may activate different aspects of our identity, even without changing countries. Workplace influence Even career or employment switches can shape people’s personality, as a growing body of research suggests that our jobs are not just an expression of who we are, but can also influence who we become. For example, a longitudinal study tracking Australian workers over five years found that moving into more senior managerial and professional roles was associated with increases in openness to experience, while another study examining nearly 7,700 German workers found that occupational demands were associated with subsequent personality development, particularly among those who remained in their jobs long enough to be shaped by them. Likewise, a longitudinal study following people from age 18 to 26 found that work experiences and personality influenced each other, such that people tended to select jobs compatible with their existing traits, but those same jobs subsequently reinforced or modified their personalities. In other words, we may choose our careers based on our personalities, but our careers can also end up choosing the personalities we develop. Of all these patterns of change, the most salient is the positive impact that environmental and cultural switches have on openness to experience, the academic term for intellectual and experiential curiosity. Interestingly, the effect is a form of “snowballing” whereby cultures operate in a way that accentuate who people are in the first place. In other words, our choices are a function of our inherent or a priori preferences and dispositions, and they contribute to augmenting them. This is why when people change, the most common outcome is that they become a more exaggerated version of their earlier selves. Psychologists have long documented the phenomenon of niche-picking, whereby people gravitate towards environments, relationships, and experiences that are compatible with their existing personalities. Importantly, this is not just a matter of selecting environments that suit us, but also being shaped by them, as illustrated by a longitudinal study showing that the personality traits that predispose people to certain work experiences tend to be reinforced by those same experiences over time. In other words, curious people may seek intellectually stimulating environments that make them even more curious, while competitive individuals may gravitate towards demanding, high-pressure cultures that further amplify their competitiveness. Thus, we don’t just choose environments that reflect who we are; we also become more like the environments we choose. Paradoxically, then, the more we change, the more we become like ourselves.

    Perhaps even more intriguingly, a series of four studies examining Spanish-English bilinguals found that people’s reported personality characteristics varied depending on the language they were using. Specifically, participants tended to report higher levels of extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness when responding in English rather than Spanish, consistent with the cultural norms associated with each language. This suggests that our personality is not always expressed in the same way across situations, and that simply switching languages may activate different aspects of our identity, even without changing countries.

    Even career or employment switches can shape people’s personality, as a growing body of research suggests that our jobs are not just an expression of who we are, but can also influence who we become. For example, a longitudinal study tracking Australian workers over five years found that moving into more senior managerial and professional roles was associated with increases in openness to experience, while another study examining nearly 7,700 German workers found that occupational demands were associated with subsequent personality development, particularly among those who remained in their jobs long enough to be shaped by them. Likewise, a longitudinal study following people from age 18 to 26 found that work experiences and personality influenced each other, such that people tended to select jobs compatible with their existing traits, but those same jobs subsequently reinforced or modified their personalities. In other words, we may choose our careers based on our personalities, but our careers can also end up choosing the personalities we develop.

    According to recent reports, of all these patterns of change, the most salient is the positive impact that environmental and cultural switches have on openness to experience, the academic term for intellectual and experiential curiosity. Interestingly, the effect is a form of “snowballing” whereby cultures operate in a way that accentuate who people are in the first place. In other words, our choices are a function of our inherent or a priori preferences and dispositions, and they contribute to augmenting them. This is why when people change, the most common outcome is that they become a more exaggerated version of their earlier selves.

    Sources indicate that psychologists have long documented the phenomenon of niche-picking, whereby people gravitate towards environments, relationships, and experiences that are compatible with their existing personalities. Importantly, this is not just a matter of selecting environments that suit us, but also being shaped by them, as illustrated by a longitudinal study showing that the personality traits that predispose people to certain work experiences tend to be reinforced by those same experiences over time. In other words, curious people may seek intellectually stimulating environments that make them even more curious, while competitive individuals may gravitate towards demanding, high-pressure cultures that further amplify their competitiveness. Thus, we don’t just choose environments that reflect who we are; we also become more like the environments we choose. Paradoxically, then, the more we change, the more we become like ourselves.

    • Previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar.
    • In a recent development, the tabs remain Home, Plan, Billing, Shop, and Support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.

    Previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar. With the network switching upgrade unveiled last week, Google Fi now has a floating navigation toolbar.

    In a recent development, the tabs remain Home, Plan, Billing, Shop, and Support. A pill-shaped tab indicator is leveraged, while there’s a prominent shadow effect. Given the floating nature, you see what’s around the toolbar, while Fi Wireless now extends underneath the system navigation bar.

    However, the Shop tab loads a webpage as before, resulting in a gap and wasted space.

    There’s now a floating action button for the new Google AI-powered Ask Fi chatbot. It provides “instant account help and troubleshooting.” If you ask for human support, the contents of the conversation carry over.

    This redesign is rolling out with version 171 of the app as a server-side update. Google Fi joins Google Photos, Chat, and Pixel Now Playing in adopting floating navigation, which is likely the newly introduced first-party mandate for a more edge-to-edge design.

    Secondary network switching is not yet widely available, with Google telling us last week that it’s a gradual rollout. The MVNO is also ending Pixel exclusivity for Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ with availability on “select” Samsung and Motorola phones.

    Sources indicate that FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

    Check out 9to5Google on YouTube for more news:.

    According to recent reports, editor-in-chief. Interested in the minutiae of Google and Alphabet. Tips/talk: abner@9to5g.com.

    #161533. Breaking: Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data reveals

    Breaking: Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data reveals

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing.
    • Recent findings suggest that every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing.
    • Industry observers note that that’s very worrying.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing. Women are disproportionately impacted yet are hugely underrepresented in AI roles, not making the decisions that have such an impact on the world. The latest comes from LinkedIn, whose recent research found that women accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025, against 50% of hires into non-AI occupations. Across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies. Thus, they make up a ridiculously small percentage of the best-paid jobs in the economy. That’s very worrying. The people designing these tools and running these companies decide what the technology is for, whose tasks get automated, and how the value is captured. If women are left out at every stage, the products and the profits will reflect it. The gender gap will get bigger because of that. But after reading some of these studies, I’ve started to wonder if they don’t also have a few blind spots of their own. In denouncing women’s absence from AI, we may fall into the old habit of downplaying what women actually already contribute because it happens in places we don’t count and fail to see. I interviewed Sarah Steinberg, who leads global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, at the Reykjavík Global Forum this week. Steinberg told me LinkedIn’s research on AI leadership highlights women are more likely to hold jobs exposed to AI and less likely to have AI skills. But do the numbers fully capture women’s AI contribution? She agreed we may be underestimating women in AI leadership. And we had just been in a session in which many women leaders from across the globe had talked about AI from another angle: regulating it, contesting it, limiting its costs for communities and the environment. These women show that many are involved in initiatives shaping the future of AI. A narrow definition of AI work The first blind spot is in the definition. LinkedIn counts someone as “AI talent” if they hold an AI-classified occupation or list two or more AI engineering skills. There may be a will to also count “implied skills”, i.e. for people in occupations that assume AI expertise even if they haven’t tagged it on their profile, but by and large the lens remains mainly technical. Women’s share of C-suite roles held by AI talent at AI companies is said to be 13%. But it leaves out government and civil society as well as leaders within the AI industry who don’t hold technical titles. Skills raise the same question. LinkedIn separates AI literacy, meaning the use of tools like ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot, from the engineering skills needed to build the technology. Asked where AI governance or policy expertise fits, Steinberg said she didn’t know whether it is counted at all, “because it’s not necessarily a technical engineering skill or a tool that you would be using.” We have seen this before. The previous generation of tech jobs was measured with coding as the yardstick, and women who ran product, policy, or trust and safety teams barely indicated up in the count. Decisions made from the outside If leadership means making decisions that change the course of AI, many of those decisions are now made outside AI companies. On Nov. 3, voters in 10 U.S. states weighed in on 41 local ballot measures related to data centers, nearly all of which aimed at limiting construction. Voters approved nearly all of them. And women are prominent in these fights. A survey found that 55% of women strongly oppose data centers, compared with 43% of men. In Prince George’s County, Maryland, Taylor Frazier McCollum’s petition gathered more than 25,000 signatures and led to moratoriums that blocked a $5 billion project. In New York, State Senator Kristen Gonzalez sponsored a bill imposing a one-year moratorium on permits for data centers drawing more than 20 megawatts, which the legislature passed in June. The revolt is likely to change the industry. It is “forcing a lot of AI leaders to have to reflect on what they have been doing that is clearly alienating the public,” Steinberg said. When companies arrive in towns and ask local politicians to sign nondisclosure agreements, on the assumption that residents would welcome a transformative technology, “what they’re finding is that the benefits that people are experiencing from this technology are not outweighing the negatives that having a data center in their community would present,” she added. Data centers do create some jobs, she added, but “whether that is at a level that is worth it relative to the downsides is up for communities to decide.” Europe tells a similar story. Margrethe Vestager coordinated the EU’s work on the AI Act, and Lucilla Sioli, who led its drafting at the European Commission, now heads the EU AI Office. In 2024, Fortune reported that women headed more than 50 % of the 30 authorities enforcing EU data rules. It’s true that some of the best-known critics of the industry, like Timnit Gebru, did not choose to stand outside the AI industry: they were pushed out. Women end up regulating and contesting AI because public-sector, legal, and community careers are more inclusive, while the best-paid technical jobs remain largely in the hands of tech bros who perpetuate a culture that actively filters women out. The women we miss Another blind spot is usage: women may use AI more than they admit. In an experiment reported in Harvard Business Review, 1,026 engineers reviewed the same piece of Python code. When told the author had used AI, they judged that person 9% less competent, even though they rated the code itself no differently. Women paid a heavier price: a 13% drop in perceived competence, compared with 6% for men. Because of this “hidden penalty of using AI”, any measure of AI skills based on self-reporting is likely to miss all the women who choose not to mention their use and their skills. Steinberg also pointed to the skills employers now want. Demand for AI literacy grew 70% year over year on LinkedIn, but the other most sought-after skills are interpersonal: communication, negotiation, conflict management. She is bullish on women’s strengths there, but she warned that “we haven’t really figured out the code” to train, evaluate, and promote people on those skills. Until we do, that contribution will remain mostly invisible too. The case for counting differently None of this is an argument for complacency. Women should be building AI tools and running AI companies, where decisions about capital and products are made. A 13% share of C-suite AI leadership roles is a disaster. And LinkedIn’s data can help better fight this fight. Because it tracks how people move from job to job, it shows where women drop off, and the answer varies by industry. In sectors where women are well represented, the biggest drop comes between vice president and the C-suite. Where they are scarce, it comes at the first manager level. In STEM, it happens in the first year after graduation, between the degree and the job. But a picture limited to engineers at AI firms makes women look absent and passive, even though many are shaping AI through ballots, legislation, regulation, and everyday use. If we could map the gap across industry, government, and civil society, we would have a better baseline, and it would probably show that women already have more say over AI than all the studies suggest.

    #161531. Tech Report: How to keep AI from turning your company into the Borg

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3215 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: How to keep AI from turning your company into the Borg

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a major fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation.
    • It has been revealed that like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a significant fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation.
    • In the show’s lore, the Borg grew by absorbing other species and their technology.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a major fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation. While I enjoyed the stories, what really stuck with me in an enduring way was the ethos of the show, and especially what it had to say about how to lead when long-term principles and immediate goals pull in different directions. The death last month of Sir Patrick Stewart—the actor behind the inimitable Captain Picard—sent me back to watch some old episodes of the show. It is perhaps unsurprising that the episodes that stood out to me were those in which the captain and his crew confronted the Borg, a collective of formerly independent life forms who had become fused together into a single hive mind. In the show’s lore, the Borg grew by absorbing other species and their technology. The hive’s drones carried the knowledge of every civilization the collective had absorbed but lacked anything in the way of individuality: they had no name, no will, and no ideas of their own. The first time I watched the episodes, I saw them as a thought-provoking and dystopian fantasy. Today, they strike me as delivering an essential warning about the dangers of AI. The Borg chased perfection through uniformity. AI seems to be sending humans along a similar, worrying trajectory. The homogenizing effect of AI Language models are trained to predict the most likely next word in a sequence, then tuned to give the kinds of answers people rate highly. The result is output that is fluent, competent, and increasingly alike. And when millions of people and thousands of companies lean on the same few models, that sameness spreads. In a 2025 study named after the Borg’s defining image of a hivemind, researchers tested more than 70 language models on real-world, open-ended questions. They found striking similarities both within models and between models—individual models repeated themselves, while groups of models collectively converged on the same responses. For example, when 25 models (from the US, China, and elsewhere) were asked 50 times to provide a metaphor about time, most of the responses were variants of time being either a river or a weaver. By contrast, when a reporter at the MIT Technology Review asked six of their (human) colleagues the same thing, they got six different answers with nary a mention of rivers or weavers. This commonality reaches beyond the texts that LLMs output themselves. In September this year, Nature rounded up a fast-growing body of research suggesting that generative AI is homogenizing how humans write, and possibly how we think. In one study it cited, students who used ChatGPT on creative tasks for just five days were still giving more similar answers months later, even when they didn’t use AI. Business is showing early signs of the same phenomenon. A recent study of earnings-call transcripts found that companies’ prepared remarks have grown strikingly similar as AI writing tools have spread, and that more uniform language was associated with more negative initial market reactions. The irony is striking. Each firm is betting that AI will make it sharper. But collectively AI seems to be making business duller and more standardized. The leaders who win in this newly introduced world will be those who find ways to capture the benefits AI can offer to individuals without falling into the trap of becoming part of the collective. Picard’s encounters with the Borg offer three lessons in how to do that. Don’t become a mouthpiece In “The Best of Both Worlds,” the Borg capture Picard and turn him into a drone they call Locutus, their spokesman. Picard’s face and voice announce decisions that are no longer his, but that come instead from the collective hivemind. Leaders may already be drifting in this direction. In IBM’s 2026 CEO study of 2,000 CEOs, 64% said they are “comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI-generated input.” Further, they expect AI to make 48% of operational decisions without human intervention by 2030, up from 25% today. Unchecked delegation to AI can end up being very expensive. In October 2025, Deloitte Australia agreed to partially refund the roughly $290,000 it was paid for a government report that contained apparent AI-generated errors such as imaginary research and made-up quotes from federal courts. More insiduously, the skills that let leaders catch such errors can fade swiftly. In a randomized trial published by Anthropic in January, developers who learned a new programming tool with AI assistance scored 17% lower on a quiz about the tool than those who had acquired their knowledge by themselves. Deloitte itself is a case in point. Last month, a year after that first refund, the government of Western Australia demanded an expedited refund from Deloitte for a study on merging three of the state’s universities. The firm had disclosed using generative AI to help gather research, summarize information, and proofread content, but the report nevertheless turned out to contain errors such as a simple miscalculation that reduced cost estimates by 260 million AUD, references to sources that did not exist, and using a name for one of the universities that had been “changed under an act of state parliament in 2017.” The takeaway: Delegate the analysis, keep the judgment. Anyone who signs off on an AI recommendation should be able to explain why it is right—and this should extend to personal ownership of all the constituent details. Protect the people who disagree The Borg instantiated the promise of a certain type of harmony: no drone ever argued with the collective for the simple reason that there was nothing to argue about. All drones thought the same thoughts and held exactly the same beliefs. This made the Borg both formidably efficient and dangerously blind. AI can build a version of that consensus into an organization. A recent Stanford-led study found that 11 leading AI systems affirmed owners’ actions 49% more frequently than did other humans, even when those actions involved deception or harm. A single affirming response made people more convinced they were right and less willing to take responsibility for their decision. Worse, participants rated flattering and non-flattering responses as about equally objective. “The very feature that causes harm also drives engagement,” the authors wrote. An organization in which every manager has a tireless assistant telling them they’re right is an organization slowly losing its capacity to disagree. On the show, the Borg’s uniformity is eventually broken by a single drone. Rescued by Picard’s crew, a drone they name Hugh develops a sense of self, and after he is sent home, this threat to the collective spreads to other drones.Yet left without support, the newly independent drones quickly fall under the control of a manipulative new leader. Independent thinking is both contagious and fragile. The takeaway: If your AI tends to agree with you, you will need to turn to other people for disagreement. Treat dissent as infrastructure. Reward the person who pushes back, and back them when they are right. Individuality without support is easily undermined. Rebuilding takes more than retraining The crew rescues Picard from the Borg quickly but it takes him much longer to become himself again. After being rescued, he goes home to his family’s vineyard in France, unsure who he is and tempted to quit Starfleet. No debriefing or new assignment puts him back together. His brother does, in a quarrel that ends with Picard finally breaking down. It takes time, and it takes family. When companies plan for what AI will do to their people, they tend to plan for skills: who needs retraining, and on which tools. Far less attention goes to the meaning and purpose that people find in work. A study published in March found that people who relied passively on AI to do their work found less meaning in it, and that the loss appeared to carry over into the work they later did on their own. And in an October survey by Elon University, 70% of U.S. workers said paid work is extremely or very important to their sense of meaning and purpose, and 65% of Americans agreed that if AI makes work less meaningful, people will lose their sense of purpose and dignity. As with Picard, much of the rebuilding happens through people. In the same survey, workers said that if AI substantially affects their jobs, they would place more faith in the people close to them than in formal organizations. Yet AI is quietly thinning those relationships at work. A recent piece in Harvard Business Review that surveyed just over 1,000 U.S. workers reported that AI was reducing communication within teams and thereby significantly reducing team trust and coordination. So the bonds are fraying just as people need them more than ever before. The takeaway: Budget for rebuilding purpose alongside retraining. Give people time to adjust, and protect the relationships they will lean on while they do. Track whether people still find meaning in their work as carefully as you track whether they can use the tools. Resistance is the point The Borg’s catchphrase was “Resistance is futile.” Patrick Stewart’s Picard proved them wrong, mostly by being stubbornly, unmistakably himself. And in that lies a crucial lesson for business leaders. AI is a remarkably useful tool. But it nudges everyone who uses it toward the same safe answer, and a company that stops noticing will end up thinking, sounding, and deciding like everyone else. Pushing back against that pull is now part of a leader’s job. Nobody else is going to do it.

    It has been revealed that like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a significant fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation. While I enjoyed the stories, what really stuck with me in an enduring way was the ethos of the show, and especially what it had to say about how to lead when long-term principles and immediate goals pull in different directions. The death last month of Sir Patrick Stewart—the actor behind the inimitable Captain Picard—sent me back to watch some old episodes of the show. It is perhaps unsurprising that the episodes that stood out to me were those in which the captain and his crew confronted the Borg, a collective of formerly independent life forms who had become fused together into a single hive mind.

    In the show’s lore, the Borg grew by absorbing other species and their technology. The hive’s drones carried the knowledge of every civilization the collective had absorbed but lacked anything in the way of individuality: they had no name, no will, and no ideas of their own. The first time I watched the episodes, I saw them as a thought-provoking and dystopian fantasy. Today, they strike me as delivering an essential warning about the dangers of AI.

    According to recent reports, the Borg chased perfection through uniformity. AI seems to be sending humans along a similar, worrying trajectory.

    Industry observers note that language models are trained to predict the most likely next word in a sequence, then tuned to give the kinds of answers people rate highly. The result is output that is fluent, competent, and increasingly alike. And when millions of people and thousands of companies lean on the same few models, that sameness spreads.

    In a 2025 study named after the Borg’s defining image of a hivemind, researchers tested more than 70 language models on real-world, open-ended questions. They found striking similarities both within models and between models—individual models repeated themselves, while groups of models collectively converged on the same responses. For example, when 25 models (from the US, China, and elsewhere) were asked 50 times to provide a metaphor about time, most of the responses were variants of time being either a river or a weaver. By contrast, when a reporter at the MIT Technology Review asked six of their (human) colleagues the same thing, they got six different answers with nary a mention of rivers or weavers.

    In a recent development, this commonality reaches beyond the texts that LLMs output themselves. In September this year, Nature rounded up a fast-growing body of research suggesting that generative AI is homogenizing how humans write, and possibly how we think. In one study it cited, students who used ChatGPT on creative tasks for just five days were still giving more similar answers months later, even when they didn’t use AI. Business is showing early signs of the same phenomenon. A recent study of earnings-call transcripts found that companies’ prepared remarks have grown strikingly similar as AI writing tools have spread, and that more uniform language was associated with more negative initial market reactions.

    Industry observers note that the irony is striking. Each firm is betting that AI will make it sharper. But collectively AI seems to be making business duller and more standardized. The leaders who win in this new world will be those who find ways to capture the benefits AI can offer to individuals without falling into the trap of becoming part of the collective. Picard’s encounters with the Borg offer three lessons in how to do that.

    Recent findings suggest that in “The Best of Both Worlds,” the Borg capture Picard and turn him into a drone they call Locutus, their spokesman. Picard’s face and voice announce decisions that are no longer his, but that come instead from the collective hivemind.

    Leaders may already be drifting in this direction. In IBM’s 2026 CEO study of 2,000 CEOs, 64% said they are “comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI-generated input.” Further, they expect AI to make 48% of operational decisions without human intervention by 2030, up from 25% today.

    Unchecked delegation to AI can end up being very expensive. In October 2025, Deloitte Australia agreed to partially refund the roughly $290,000 it was paid for a government report that contained apparent AI-generated errors such as imaginary research and made-up quotes from federal courts.

    According to recent reports, more insiduously, the skills that let leaders catch such errors can fade swiftly. In a randomized trial published by Anthropic in January, developers who learned a fresh programming tool with AI assistance scored 17% lower on a quiz about the tool than those who had acquired their knowledge by themselves. Deloitte itself is a case in point. Last month, a year after that first refund, the government of Western Australia demanded an expedited refund from Deloitte for a study on merging three of the state’s universities. The firm had disclosed using generative AI to help gather research, summarize information, and proofread content, but the report nevertheless turned out to contain errors such as a simple miscalculation that reduced cost estimates by 260 million AUD, references to sources that did not exist, and using a name for one of the universities that had been “changed under an act of state parliament in 2017.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the takeaway: Delegate the analysis, keep the judgment. Anyone who signs off on an AI recommendation should be able to explain why it is right—and this should extend to personal ownership of all the constituent details.

    It has been revealed that the Borg instantiated the promise of a certain type of harmony: no drone ever argued with the collective for the simple reason that there was nothing to argue about. All drones thought the same thoughts and held exactly the same beliefs. This made the Borg both formidably efficient and dangerously blind.

    AI can build a version of that consensus into an organization. A recent Stanford-led study found that 11 leading AI systems affirmed users’ actions 49% more frequently than did other humans, even when those actions involved deception or harm. A single affirming response made people more convinced they were right and less willing to take responsibility for their decision. Worse, participants rated flattering and non-flattering responses as about equally objective. “The very feature that causes harm also drives engagement,” the authors wrote. An organization in which every manager has a tireless assistant telling them they’re right is an organization slowly losing its capacity to disagree.

    On the show, the Borg’s uniformity is eventually broken by a single drone. Rescued by Picard’s crew, a drone they name Hugh develops a sense of self, and after he is sent home, this threat to the collective spreads to other drones.Yet left without support, the newly independent drones promptly fall under the control of a manipulative new leader. Independent thinking is both contagious and fragile.

    The takeaway: If your AI tends to agree with you, you will need to turn to other people for disagreement. Treat dissent as infrastructure. Reward the person who pushes back, and back them when they are right. Individuality without support is easily undermined.

    Recent findings suggest that the crew rescues Picard from the Borg quickly but it takes him much longer to become himself again. After being rescued, he goes home to his family’s vineyard in France, unsure who he is and tempted to quit Starfleet. No debriefing or latest assignment puts him back together. His brother does, in a quarrel that ends with Picard finally breaking down. It takes time, and it takes family.

    When companies strategy for what AI will do to their people, they tend to plan for skills: who needs retraining, and on which tools. Far less attention goes to the meaning and purpose that people find in work. A study published in March found that people who relied passively on AI to do their work found less meaning in it, and that the loss appeared to carry over into the work they later did on their own. And in an October survey by Elon University, 70% of U.S. workers remarked paid work is extremely or very important to their sense of meaning and purpose, and 65% of Americans agreed that if AI makes work less meaningful, people will lose their sense of purpose and dignity.

    In a recent development, as with Picard, much of the rebuilding happens through people. In the same survey, workers noted that if AI substantially affects their jobs, they would place more faith in the people close to them than in formal organizations. Yet AI is quietly thinning those relationships at work. A recent piece in Harvard Business Review that surveyed just over 1,000 U.S. workers reported that AI was reducing communication within teams and thereby significantly reducing team trust and coordination. So the bonds are fraying just as people need them more than ever before.

    Recent findings suggest that the takeaway: Budget for rebuilding purpose alongside retraining. Give people time to adjust, and protect the relationships they will lean on while they do. Track whether people still find meaning in their work as carefully as you track whether they can use the tools.

    It has been revealed that the Borg’s catchphrase was “Resistance is futile.” Patrick Stewart’s Picard proved them wrong, mostly by being stubbornly, unmistakably himself. And in that lies a crucial lesson for business leaders.

    AI is a remarkably useful tool. But it nudges everyone who uses it toward the same safe answer, and a company that stops noticing will end up thinking, sounding, and deciding like everyone else. Pushing back against that pull is now part of a leader’s job. Nobody else is going to do it.

    ‘Sex sells, fellas’: President Trump defends Jensen Huang, says he pushed for him to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that president Donald Trump says he played a role in pushing Nvidia to reinstate company president and CEO Jensen Huang.
    • President Donald Trump claims he played a role in pushing Nvidia to reinstate tech giant president and CEO Jensen Huang.
    • On Monday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang would resume his position just 11 days after the tech mogul’s resignation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that president Donald Trump says he played a role in pushing Nvidia to reinstate company president and CEO Jensen Huang. On Monday morning, Nvidia revealed that Huang would resume his position just 11 days after the tech mogul’s resignation. “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang mentioned in a statement on the latest development. The decision comes as multiple investigations—including those from the Justice Department and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission—are still ongoing. And just last week, Nvidia chairman Harvey ​Jones had said that the company would not rehire Huang, given that his conduct did not meet the company’s code of conduct. Huang had stepped down as CEO after allegedly having an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as an additional affair with a subordinate. But after Monday’s stunning decision to reinstate Huang, Trump seemingly took some credit for the move, telling the media that he advocated for the briefly jobless boss to come back into power. Trump told CNBC that Huang “did nothing wrong,” and said that he spoke to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” ahead of the move, making clear that he argued on behalf of the CEO. The president also made clear that he told the company that Huang returning to his role was the best decision in terms of national security, and for winning the AI race with adversaries like China. “They did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” Trump told the outlet. He added: “People say, ‘Is it a threat to have him?’ No, it’s a threat to lose him.” When asked about Huang’s extramarital activities, Trump even went so far as to say the ordeal would help, rather than hurt, the CEO’s success. “I think he’s going to start off at an almost higher level,” the president said. “He’s apologized for the indiscretions, which were unfortunate. Probably, that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas.” With this remark, Trump seemed to imply that the nature of the news story being tied to affairs is what brought it so much attention.The president seemed to double down on the sentiment on Truth Social by posting an image of Huang waving a Photoshopped red bra in the air, referencing a famous photo from the 2024 assassination attempt on Trump’s life in Pennsylvania. Trump may have been the most influential voice, but he wasn’t the only powerful person standing behind Huang. An open letter to Nvidia’s board titled “Stand With Jensen” had gained more than 206,000 signatures as of Monday morning. One of them was from Elon Musk, who took to X to share that he had signed it on November 13. “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I’m signing it too,” the Tesla and SpaceX CEO wrote. More than 10,000 of the signers said they were current Nvidia employees, while more than 108,000 said they were shareholders. Still, while the White House and tech moguls may be behind the decision, Huang’s critics aren’t staying quiet. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X that Trump is “putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security.” Some Republicans even came out against Huang’s reinstatement, including Sen. John Cornyn of Texas. In response to Trump’s denial that the affair posed any risks, the outgoing GOP senator posted on X: “No national security risk? Based on what?” However, in the wake of his reinstatement, experts are now saying it was almost inevitable, given just how irreplaceable the CEO seemed to be. “There were definitely a lot of people who wanted him back. The extent that the administration intervened, the extent that shareholders intervened—it ​will be impossible to know,” said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, per Reuters. Sosnick added: “But it tells us to some extent that Jensen Huang was too big to be fired.”Nvidia’s stocks were up 30% in the hours after Monday’s major announcement.

    Motorola’s Razr Flex has leaked in full, with the iPhone Duo competitor showing off its wide form factor in two colors, and it looks great.

    Following a leaker earlier this morning, SammyGuru has published newly introduced images of the Razr Flex, an iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor that Motorola has been teasing for months now.

    These images show the “Dark Botanical Garden” green and “Coriander” brown with woven and leather-like backplates, two rear-facing cameras, and selfie cameras on both displays. The outer display, remarked to be 4.97 inches, is wide but very compact, while the inner display is wide in the same way that the iPhone Duo is. The inner panel is expected to be around 7 inches in size.

    SammyGuru mentions that the hinge can hold itself half-open and that the price might come in at around $1,799 – though any guesses here are up in the air in the age of RAMageddon.

    Motorola Razr Flex is expected to launch in early 2027, with CES in January being a very likely launch timeline for the new foldable.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in a stunning turnaround, Nvidia’s board reinstated ousted founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, president, and as a member of the board, effective immediately on Monday, sending Nvidia’s (Nasdaq: NVDA) stock soaring over 30% along with a host of memory chip stocks. Given Nvidia’s position as a leader in artificial intelligence, the news had a ripple effect in the infrastructure and networking AI space. Shares of a number of memory and storage stocks were up double digits on Monday morning as of this writing: Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU) up over 19% Sandisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK) up 16% Western Digital Corporation (Nasdaq: WDC) up 14% Seagate Technology Holdings (Nasdaq: STX) up 14% Neoclouds float back to the sky And that’s not all. Shares of neocloud providers CoreWeave, Inc. (Nasdaq: NCRWV) rose over 22%, while shares Nebius Group N.V. (Nasdaq: NBIS) jumped 24%. To be fair, technology stocks were already rebounding before news hit on Monday—after last week’s sharp sell-off, which saw all three major market averages end in a correction by Friday. By Monday morning, many investors apparently saw an opportunity to buy low. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) was up 5% after seven brutal days of declines, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose 3%, and the Nasdaq (^IXIC) was up 6.8%, at the time of this writing Monday afternoon, according to Yahoo Finance. “The market’s explosive reaction reflects just how critical Huang is to investor confidence, and I believe his reinstatement could serve as a catalyst for a much broader recovery in AI related stocks,” David Miller, CIO and senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds, tells Fast Organization. “While questions remain about the ultimate returns on massive AI capital expenditures, today’s announcement meaningfully improves sentiment and reduces a major risk that had been hanging over the sector.” The reversal—both in the market gains and Jensen Huang’s luck—is just the latest chapter in the Nvidia cofounder’s ongoing drama that reads straight out of a spy thriller. The saga is complete with not one, not two, but three alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman feared to be working for Chinese intelligence. It comes less than two weeks after Huang’s resignation, and after President Donald Trump noted on Monday that he spoke to Nvidia’s board about reinstating Huang. “I believe my intervention was very important . . . I convinced them . . . I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC Monday morning, adding Huang “did nothing wrong.”.

    #161521. Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2829 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

    Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather.
    • The Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather.
    • Strogatz is no ordinary mathematician.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather. Yet for almost two centuries, a central question about them remained unsolved. We knew the equations worked in practice, but no one had proven whether they always hold up mathematically without breaking down.That all changed in September when OpenAI claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes problem, followed on October 6 by a torrent of proposed breakthroughs across nearly 400 math problems that had baffled researchers for generations. As Cornell University mathematician Steven Strogatz explained in an Atlantic essay, the announcements have left the field reeling. How should people think about their work when a machine can do it so much better? Strogatz is no ordinary mathematician. A pioneer in the field of nonlinear systems and network science, he is also an award-winning author and a sometime Latest York Times columnist. His livelihood is not in danger. Yet OpenAI has him asking, “What’s the point?” It’s a question we’re all going to have to answer. Here are three principles that will help you figure it out. Principle 1: The Infinite Monkey Theorem The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges had a fascination with a concept known as the infinite monkey theorem. The idea is that if you had an infinite number of monkeys pecking away at an infinite number of typewriters, they would randomly create the collected works of Tolstoy and every other masterwork ever written (or that could be written). Clearly, today we are living in our own version of the infinite monkey theorem, which is what Strogatz was getting at in his Atlantic piece. If you can have infinite agents attacking every aspect of an age-old problem, solving it over a period of hours, what is the value of a mathematician’s work? Is it even worth pursuing? Borges, in his story The Library of Babel, gave us—and mathematicians like Strogatz—some guidance about creating value in a world of infinite monkeys. First, there is the problem of curation. Yes, infinite monkeys could write War and Peace, but good luck finding it amongst all the flotsam and jetsam. We’re seeing the problem in real life today. While AI should theoretically be ramping up productivity, in reality, workers are drowning in workslop. The second problem is that of intent. War and Peace isn’t just meaningful for the words it contains, but because of what Leo Tolstoy intended when he wrote them. In much the same way, while it is true that artificial intelligence can run circles around human mathematicians, it is also true that humans chose the problems that OpenAI solved, and they chose them because humans found them meaningful and, possibly, useful. So one way that mathematicians—or anyone else—can find meaning and value in the age of AI is by acting as curators and as principal agents. Humans can choose the work that gets done according to what is meaningful to them and other humans. You could see the seeds of that idea in Strogatz’s piece. Even if all problems are solvable, we still need to choose which ones we want to solve. Principle 2: The economics of automation Another way to think about how you find meaning and create value in the age of AI is to analyze the economics of automation. One effective framework involves examining three constituent forces: the displacement effect, the productivity effect, and the reinstatement effect. Together, they can help us determine where threats and opportunities might lie. The displacement effect refers to jobs that are replaced by an automating technology—in this case, AI. The productivity effect refers to the increase in output per given unit of input due to the technological advance. The reinstatement effect refers to new jobs made possible by a technological advance. To understand how the three effects work together, it’s helpful to look at the life of Henry Ford. Growing up on a family farm, young Henry would once have been expected to remain in the fields. But as agricultural productivity increased, he had more opportunities beyond the farm. He eventually went to work for Thomas Edison and later created an entirely new automobile industry, reinstating millions of jobs both directly and indirectly. In the case of Henry Ford, the story was a happy one. The productivity and reinstatement effects dwarfed the displacement effect and everybody, for the most part, was better off. But the AI data is fuzzy. We are certainly seeing early signs of the displacement effect as people lose jobs, but so far we’ve seen few signs of a significant productivity or reinstatement effect. Still, understanding the economics of automation can help us find value and meaning. Clearly, with answers to tough problems so much more accessible, mathematicians—and other experts—can help the rest of us formulate good problems to apply to real-world challenges. Some value will likely shift from solving problems to finding good questions. 3. Jevons Paradox and the O-Ring model During the Industrial Revolution—which the AI age is often compared to—James Watt’s steam engine used coal much more efficiently than Thomas Newcomen’s version. So, many assumed that coal use would go down. But English economist William Stanley Jevons saw that just the opposite was happening. Coal use was actually increasing. Ever since, that phenomenon has been known as the Jevons paradox, the effect that occurs when technological improvements that increase the efficiency of a resource’s use lead to a rise, rather than a fall, in its use. If price elasticity is high enough, the decrease in costs encourages people to find more uses for that resource and demand increases. Another useful concept is the O-ring theory of economic development, which gets its name from the Challenger space shuttle disaster. The shuttle, for the most part, was in good working order, but a malfunction in an O-ring seal due to unusually cold weather led to a massive midair explosion. The point is that every job is made up of many interdependent tasks, and if even a single one fails, the entire thing doesn’t work. We’re seeing signs of both effects in the AI economy. While software developers can outsource many coding tasks to AI, they still need humans for others, such as communicating and collaborating with other experts on the team. Nevertheless, with code being produced so much more efficiently, job postings for software developers are on the rise. Strogatz may find something similar happening in mathematics. After all, there are many facets of his job that don’t involve developing proofs. He is a teacher, a writer, and an incredible translator of complex mathematical concepts for laypeople. Maybe more mathematicians can follow suit,  helping experts in other fields solve important problems with mathematical insights. The future of technology is always more human Technological revolutions are always fraught, with plenty of optimism, anxiety, and visions of doom to go around. A breakthrough proves to be transformational, attracting investment that overestimates the opportunity. Boom leads to bust. Jobs are displaced, then new ones appear and, at some point, we look back and it all seems as if it were preordained. Yet when you’re in the midst of disruption, there is little comfort. Yes, things tend to work out in the aggregate, but many are often left worse off. In fact, despite all of the incredible technological advances of the last half-century, a 2018 Pew Research study found that Americans’ real incomes have remained essentially unchanged, with many households far worse off. Today, there is no shortage of opinions about where AI is taking us. Tech entrepreneurs claim that we are on the brink of such a productivity boom that it will lead to a new age of abundance—if, of course, it doesn’t kill us. Economists are much more muted, seeing meager gains amid massive overinvestment. Yet for most of us, those macro-trends aren’t nearly as important as how AI will affect us—and our well-being—directly. The good news is that we have good tools to help us navigate our way through. The infinite monkey theorem highlights the importance of curation and intent. The economics of automation reveals the need for productivity growth to finance reinstatement. The Jevons paradox and the O-ring model encourage us to identify our place within increasingly complex ecosystems. AI can give us answers, but it can’t tell us what questions we want to ask. In the future, that’s where human value and meaning will increasingly lie.

He is a teacher, a writer, and an incredible translator of complex mathematical concepts for laypeople. Maybe more mathematicians can follow suit,  helping experts in other fields solve key problems with mathematical insights.

    Technological revolutions are always fraught, with plenty of optimism, anxiety, and visions of doom to go around. A breakthrough proves to be transformational, attracting investment that overestimates the opportunity. Boom leads to bust. Jobs are displaced, then new ones appear and, at some point, we look back and it all seems as if it were preordained.

    Recent findings suggest that yet when you’re in the midst of disruption, there is little comfort. Yes, things tend to work out in the aggregate, but many are often left worse off. In fact, despite all of the incredible technological advances of the last half-century, a 2018 Pew Research study found that Americans’ real incomes have remained essentially unchanged, with many households far worse off.

    Today, there is no shortage of opinions about where AI is taking us. Tech entrepreneurs claim that we are on the brink of such a productivity boom that it will lead to a upcoming age of abundance—if, of course, it doesn’t kill us. Economists are much more muted, seeing meager gains amid massive overinvestment. Yet for most of us, those macro-trends aren’t nearly as notable as how AI will affect us—and our well-being—directly.

    Sources indicate that the good news is that we have good tools to help us navigate our way through. The infinite monkey theorem highlights the importance of curation and intent. The economics of automation reveals the need for productivity growth to finance reinstatement. The Jevons paradox and the O-ring model encourage us to identify our place within increasingly complex ecosystems.

    It has been revealed that AI can give us answers, but it can’t tell us what questions we want to ask. In the future, that’s where human value and meaning will increasingly lie.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available.
    • Canva today confirmed “AI Controls,” a latest toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.
    • Generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available. If you’ve ever wanted to just turn off AI features, Canva proves that it could be a simple toggle, if companies actually wanted to give you a choice.

    Canva today confirmed “AI Controls,” a latest toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.

    Generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference. Canva puts this well:.

    In a recent development, for some people, AI is the most exciting creative tool in a generation, while others prefer bringing their ideas to life without it. We believe the future of creativity should give everyone the freedom to choose their own path, whether that’s creating with AI, without it, or somewhere in between.

    Sources indicate that to give its users the choice, Canva’s Permissions menu now has a simple toggle for “Enable Generative AI features.” Toggling it off disables features such as Magic Write and Magic Edit. There’s also an option to limit how much AI-generated imagery appears in the Canva library.

    Put simply, this is great to see.

    AI has its place, but everyone should have a choice like this, especially when it comes to apps and services used for artistry in the same vein as Canva. Yet, the tech industry continues to go in the opposite direction, shoving AI into every corner whether it’s actually useful or not. Canva proves, though, that it doesn’t have to be that way.

    A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report shows two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

    Recent findings suggest that both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

    According to recent reports, A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

    This tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

    Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

    Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

    In a recent development, this separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

    For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

    Keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

    Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

    Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:.

    According to recent reports, run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

    Sources indicate that keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

    Recent findings suggest that treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

    Industry observers note that missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

    Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

    There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

    Recent findings suggest that providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

    Keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

    Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

    In a recent development, caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

    A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:.

    "occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",.

    "data": { "status": "completed" }.

    According to recent reports, the event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

    Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

    The following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

    According to recent reports, resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

    According to recent reports, for a form, issue a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a latest one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

    It has been revealed that twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

    Authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

    Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM upgrade. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

    In a recent development, A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

    It has been revealed that here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

    received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),.

    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id).

    FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id).

    REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id).
