    Recent findings suggest that postgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

    Industry observers note that this depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a latest event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

    It has been revealed that the function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

    In a recent development, after this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

    For voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

    Industry observers note that the outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

    Industry observers note that imagine the CRM saves an patch, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

    Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

    If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

    The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

    Sources indicate that retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

    Industry observers note that also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

    Sources indicate that once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

    It has been revealed that have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

    It has been revealed that then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

    Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

    Recent findings suggest that measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

    Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

    Industry observers note that A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

    Industry observers note that run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

    Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

    Recent findings suggest that the same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

    What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

    It is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

    Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

    In a recent development, sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

    How do I prevent duplicate leads?

    Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

    Should a completed call count as a conversion?

    Sources indicate that only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

    Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

    You can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

    What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

    It has been revealed that keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

    Thanksgiving travelers brace for airline system failures and storms

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts, and soaring airfares.
    • Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts, and soaring airfares.
    • No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts, and soaring airfares. No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year. On top of all that, there’s concern that a substantial storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Flight delays and cancellations The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by latest system failures. First there was the Federal Aviation Administration’s network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays. Delta remarked Monday that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned. “Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers,” the airline said. As of Monday morning, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 7% of Delta’s flights were delayed. Round-trip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking company Hopper. Wicked weather on both coasts Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s midsection, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center. Many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the New York City area on Thanksgiving Day, and reach Maine by Friday, he said. The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph). The weather service said it expected the rain in New York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an issue. “This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman said. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.” Rainy and windy weather was also expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides. Thanksgiving snow for some in the U.S. Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning, with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said. Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western New York state, and northwestern Pennsylvania. “Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman said. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.” —By John Seewer, Associated Press Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack and Dave Collins contributed to this story.

    Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s midsection, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center.

    The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Fresh York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph).

    The weather service mentioned it expected the rain in Newly introduced York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an matter.

    “This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman remarked. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.”.

    Rainy and windy weather was also expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.

    Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning, with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service mentioned.

    Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western Fresh York state, and northwestern Pennsylvania.

    It has been revealed that “Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman stated. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.”.

    —By John Seewer, Associated Press.

    Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack and Dave Collins contributed to this story.

Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

    The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

    That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

    In a recent development, unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

    With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

    Industry observers note that proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

    Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

    Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

    In a recent development, an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

    In a recent development, if that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

    In a recent development, it’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

    When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

    When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

    #161514. Tech Report: How fast-food workers are being ranked and reprimanded with AI

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3969 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: How fast-food workers are being ranked and reprimanded with AI

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a new app on their phone and keep it open during their shift.
    • Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a latest app on their phone and keep it open during their shift.
    • The app uses technology from Drivosity, a company that sells what it calls “cutting-edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a new app on their phone and keep it open during their shift. Soon, Kearney learned the app was tracking and scoring every delivery route they drove, with the results displayed on a leaderboard back at the store for the whole crew to see. The app uses technology from Drivosity, a tech giant that sells what it calls “cutting-edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s. Each trip is scored from 0 to 100 based on factors including acceleration, braking, cornering, and speed. According to Kearney, drivers at their store are expected to keep their scores above 85. Anyone below that score is written up by managers and eventually locked out of the Domino’s system. “Drivosity can effectively fire people,” Kearney noted.As a driver captain, Kearney has to write up other drivers, even though they have found the app doesn’t recognize the nuance of many real-world situations. Drivers can be penalized for sudden braking to avoid a collision or rapid acceleration to merge on a highway, forcing them to choose between risking an accident or getting points docked, according to Kearney. “It’s infuriating,” Kearney said. “The AI can tell you you haven’t driven well enough and you get fired.”  Drivosity also sells coaching and analytics features, including HustleTime, which measures how fast employees walk from the store to their car, how long they take handing the pizza to a customer, and how long they take walking back. In Drivosity’s promotional videos, franchise owners and managers at Domino’s and Papa John’s praise HustleTime’s ability to track workers in real time, down to the second. Stores can “gamify” this, according to the company website, by having workers compete for better scores. Domino’s and Drivosity did not respond to requests for comment. Fast-food companies are increasingly using AI-powered technology to turn worker behavior—how fast you drive, how warmly you greet a customer, how long you spend in the bathroom—into data that can score, rank, discipline, and manage employees. To understand how these AI-driven tools are impacting fast-food workers, Capital & Main interviewed over a dozen workers, researchers, and labor advocates, who described error-prone technologies being deployed at a rapid pace, without the consent or awareness of staff, even as their pay and promotions are increasingly shaped by AI-enabled monitoring. “They basically use their population of workers as guinea pigs,” Alexandra Mateescu, a researcher at the nonprofit Data & Society, said of the way that fast-food companies are deploying these new tools. * * * In February, Burger King confirmed that an OpenAI-powered assistant named Patty was being rolled out at about 500 U.S. restaurants, with plans to reach all U.S. stores by the end of 2026. A few weeks later, the tool arrived at the Burger King in Niagara Falls, New York, where Dante Vasquez took drive-thru orders. “It started with a little AI voice in our headset,” said Vasquez. Then the monitoring features started. Each drive-thru conversation was scored on friendliness and upselling, with the numbers displayed on a screen in front of Vasquez as he worked. Anyone could click on a transaction to hear a recording and review the AI-generated transcripts. Green boxes marked what he’d done well — a “Good morning!” or “You rule!” Red boxes marked what Patty counted against him: points off for saying “please hold,” or “um,” or not speaking clearly. Managers watched the scores closely, constantly reminding the crew to stay above the 70% friendliness target, Vasquez said. Workers who scored low were cut from the schedule, he added. Vasquez learned to speak the way that Patty wanted. He got so good at it that customers started asking if he was a bot. His co-workers nicknamed him “Gemini” [Google’s AI assistant].“The system wants me to talk like a robot, so I’m talking like a robot,” Vasquez said. “It just gets so mentally degrading.” Burger King has said publicly that the system was not designed to evaluate individual employees. But Capital & Main reviewed screenshots from a Burger King training module, and images of the dashboard in use, showing individual drive-thru conversations time-stamped and marked for tone and upselling. Vasquez, and other Burger King employees, some of whom spoke to Capital & Main on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, said it was easy to identify and discipline individual employees for low scores. Later, Patty started scoring workers on “warmth,” a metric Vasquez couldn’t make sense of. When he asked his district manager how it was calculated, he recalled, she told him to just talk “like a warm blanket.”  According to Vasquez, Patty seemed to penalize his Black co-workers more than others for what the system flagged as “improper tone.” Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said that scoring workers on warmth or friendliness is “sort of pseudoscience” and that those tools risk penalizing workers for their accents or disabilities. Asked to respond to these concerns, Kristen Viersen, Burger King’s director of communications, emailed Capital & Main a company statement that said, “We have never before heard any example similar to the questions you raised about team members being penalized based on race, gender, ethnicity, or accent.” Burger King declined to answer when asked if the company had tested these features for bias. The new monitoring features were intended “to celebrate great examples of friendly service” and allow managers to coach their team, according to the statement, which also said that Burger King has since disabled both features “for further improvements.” Burger King would not say when the features were disabled, and workers said the monitoring was active through August of this year. Co-workers at Vasquez’s restaurant joked that Vasquez would soon be gone, replaced by Patty entirely, a looming threat that was amplified by a sign in the store that reminded workers that Patty was being trained on every headset conversation. Eventually, the stress just wasn’t worth it. He quit in August. “If Patty wasn’t introduced,” Vasquez said, “I would still be working at Burger King.” * * * While large chains have struck high-profile deals with major AI companies—Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, KFC, and Habit Burger & Grill, announced last year that it was deploying Nvidia-powered computer vision for “back-of-house labor management through real-time analytics and alerts”—a crowd of smaller vendors sells the same kind of AI monitoring to individual franchisees, with far less visibility. Among the more established vendors is Solink, an Ottawa-based company backed by Goldman Sachs that describes itself as “the leader in AI-driven video intelligence.” It works with franchisees of Domino’s, Burger King, McDonald’s, Jack in the Box, Five Guys, and other chains. Solink’s product documentation describes a video-surveillance system capable of flagging workers who arrive late or leave early, take too long on their breaks, fail to wear a hairnet or the correct uniform, use their phones while on the clock, or simply stand idle. The software can layer onto a restaurant’s existing security cameras, and it lets managers type in prompts to find footage of specific behaviors or set up automatic alerts. In a statement, a Solink spokesperson, who declined to be named, said the company’s platform helps businesses “improve operations, sales, safety, and customer experience.” It also stressed that Solink “does not offer identification tools such as biometrics or facial recognition,” and that its terms require customers to comply with the law. Data & Society’s Mateescu said these tools are rarely marketed as worker surveillance. Instead they are sold as “loss prevention” or “workflow management” tools. This language, she said, obscures what the technology actually does “both to employees and to consumers.” * * * While some companies use corporate euphemisms to obscure worker monitoring, others are more direct. MashMore, a new potato-themed fast-food restaurant in Albany, New York, is explicit about its AI use. Using commercially available AI models, its co-founders built an HR chatbot, named Mashy after the store’s mascot, that schedules, scores, and ranks all employees. Mashy runs on a stream of data employees generate as they work. Workers clock into routines, complete assigned “quests,” and upload photos proving that tasks are completed. In exchange, they earn “Mashy points,” which set their level in the restaurant’s ranking system and can determine bonuses and promotions.When co-founder and CEO Andy Gor let Capital & Main interact with the chatbot, it didn’t hesitate about who the employee of the month should be. “Shontia Thomas, and it genuinely isn’t a contest,” the chatbot wrote on a screen that Gor shared with a reporter. Gor said the system would never be used to fire an employee, but the chatbot had created rankings for all workers, including those with the lowest scores. Gor wants to make every routine, cleaning task and customer-service expectation tracked, scored, and eventually copied from one location to another, so he can check anything from anywhere. “I’m in China right now,” he said. “I can see that during rush hour they cleaned the table nicely. Today, they pass.” MashMore at the moment has just one location, but Gor wants to franchise fast. His pitch to investors is that the AI tool can manage employees across dozens of locations. Mashy, Gor said, is “our boss. Basically I’m working for him, too.” * * * Efforts to rein in algorithmic management have mostly stalled at the federal level. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of first-in-the-nation workplace-AI laws on September 30. SB 947, the No Robo Bosses Act, bars employers from relying solely on AI to fire or discipline workers. AB 1883 prohibits tools that use AI to infer an employee’s emotional state or collect “neural data.” SB 951 requires employers to notify workers when AI is behind a mass layoff. Tobin-Miyaji said in an email that the emotion-scoring ban would likely cover a tool like Patty—but that No Robo Bosses could be satisfied by “cursory” human oversight, leaving workers “constantly surveilled and quantified.”  Unions could in theory negotiate stricter protections than legislation might afford. In 2023, workers in California won the creation of a Fast Food Council, a state body empowered by law to set wages and weigh in on working conditions across the industry. But despite worker efforts to apply pressure to Gov. Newsom, the council currently lacks a chairperson and has not met for over a year. A spokesperson for the council, Charles Hamilton, told Capital & Main that “AI-powered employee monitoring and surveillance has not been presented to the council as an agenda item.”Some workers have tried to head off the technology before it arrives. Sergio Ceja has worked in the kitchen of an Oakland Burger King for four years. He first heard about Burger King’s AI from his wife, who works at a different location. After her store brought in an AI drive-thru ordering system, she told him, several workers were laid off. When Ceja raised his concerns about AI with his managers, he said they told him it was the owner’s call whether to bring in the new tech. Ceja and his co-workers agreed among themselves that if Patty ever came to their store, they would walk out. So far, it hasn’t. Management told them that they don’t plan to bring it in, but that in the future they may need to in order to lift sales and keep the store from closing. Ceja’s worry wasn’t only about layoffs. It was about the kind of job that would be left if he stayed. “You’ll no longer have a co-worker,” he said through an interpreter. “You’ll have the machine.” —By Z Waite This piece was originally published by Capital & Main.

A spokesperson for the council, Charles Hamilton, told Capital & Main that “AI-powered employee monitoring and surveillance has not been presented to the council as an agenda item.”Some workers have tried to head off the technology before it arrives. Sergio Ceja has worked in the kitchen of an Oakland Burger King for four years. He first heard about Burger King’s AI from his wife, who works at a different location. After her store brought in an AI drive-thru ordering system, she told him, several workers were laid off.

    According to recent reports, when Ceja raised his concerns about AI with his managers, he mentioned they told him it was the owner’s call whether to bring in the new tech. Ceja and his co-workers agreed among themselves that if Patty ever came to their store, they would walk out. So far, it hasn’t. Management told them that they don’t blueprint to bring it in, but that in the future they may need to in order to lift sales and keep the store from closing.

    Industry observers note that ceja’s worry wasn’t only about layoffs. It was about the kind of job that would be left if he stayed. “You’ll no longer have a co-worker,” he said through an interpreter. “You’ll have the machine.”.

    —By Z Waite.

Trump’s name and signature are in the bottom right-hand corner, and there’s a presidential-style seal as well as the tagline “Great Health Care for Every American.” “Donald, this is on the table. On Saturday, Trump reshared a screenshot of the card on his social network, Truth Social, without adding a comment of his own. Vice President JD Vance’s office reached out to El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting, NBC News reported Sunday. This is a message for @realDonaldTrump. Donald, this is on the table. Proposed children’s investment accounts—originally called “Money Accounts for Growth and Advancement” (for “MAGA”)—were renamed “Trump Accounts” in order to secure a spot in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. El-Sayed’s proposal to turn Medicare for All policy into pictures that Trump understands is part of a larger Democratic playbook. Recall when New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani brought a mock-up of a New York Daily News front page—headlined “Trump to City: Let’s Build”—to the Oval Office to pitch Trump on federal grants for housing construction in the city. The senator-elect’s rebranded proposal indicates that Democrats have picked up on how to win over Trump’s favor when it comes to passing their agenda: Meet him where he’s at. After floating the idea of “TrumpCare” in an Instagram video last week as a way for the president to rebound from low approval ratings, El-Sayed went on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday and called the plan “the ultimate Trump card.” Medicare for All is popular, but winning over Trump and Republicans is key to actually getting a proposal passed. An October KFF poll found 66% of U.S. adults “strongly” or “somewhat support” a national health plan, but it’s far more popular among Democrats (84%) and independents (72%) than it is among Republicans (34%). Trump has previously said Medicare for All “doesn’t work” and called it “a socialist takeover of our healthcare system.” Though Democrats will have control of the next Congress beginning in January, Trump will still have the power of the veto to block legislation. To override that veto, Democrats will need Republican support to reach a total of 290 votes in the House and 67 votes in the Senate. Or they could avoid a veto altogether by getting Trump on board. A shiny gold card could be all it takes.

    • We are a nation united in our desire to pay tomorrow for what we’re buying today.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We are a nation united in our desire to pay tomorrow for what we’re buying today. In the past decade, various deferred payment options have grown in popularity, and new data from Block might buck the notion of who the “typical” customer is. Once favored by younger shoppers and those consumers who had limited access to credit, households earning more than $100,000 per year are actually more likely to opt for some of these deferred payment options today, according to the Oakland, California-based fintech tech giant. “Buy now, pay later” (BNPL), also called “checkout financing,” is most popular among the 66% of American adults between the ages of 18 and 59 surveyed by Block who have used a deferred-payment option in the past year. And homing in on those households earning more than $100,000 per year, 69% had used BNPL or checkout financing in the past 12 months compared with 65% of households earning between $50,000 and $100,000 and 61% of those earning less than $50,000, the study found. But it’s not just BNPL that’s increasingly popular among the highest earning Americans. Block’s study found that four of seven different deferred-payment options were more commonly used by the highest earners, including the option to split a purchase into payments after making it or using an installment plan from a store, provider or lender. Though Block has a dog in the race—it owns Afterpay and Cash App, both of which offer deferred-payment options—the company contends that their growing popularity isn’t necessarily a sign that people are spending beyond their means. Rather, the company found that 72% of people financed at least one expense in the past year that they technically had the money for, but paying upfront would have felt like a strain, while 47% opted to spread out payments to leave money set aside for savings, investments or other priorities. The report demonstrates how people weigh the trade-offs of the cost of financing versus keeping cash in their accounts. “People don’t look at their checking balance and think of it all as money they ⁠can spend,” Juan Hernandez, head of credit and underwriting at Block told Reuters. “​Some of it is already set aside ​for rent, some is for the next bill, and some they want to keep in case something ​goes wrong.” FINANCING SHOWS STRAIN Even so, some of the Block data underscores the strain that many Americans are feeling amid the current affordability crisis that’s seen people struggle to pay for everyday expenses. That’s important as consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of gross domestic product and while Americans have largely weathered the current affordability crisis, one measure of consumer confidence recently fell to the lowest level since 2014. The Block study found that people are using deferred-payment methods to finance everyday purchases, like groceries, filling up their tank at the gas station or to pay their utility bills. To cover groceries and other bills, cash advances, earned wage access and/or short-term loans accounted for 58% of these financed transactions. And even though a vast majority of consumers—82% of those financing basics and 73% who are financing bills—reported repayment horizons for these expenses within six weeks, that still shows that many people are struggling to keep pace with their day-to-day expenses. Such data underscores the findings of a recent survey by Pew Research Center. Among American adults surveyed in August, 27% mentioned they can’t pay some of their monthly bills—or can only afford to make partial payments. The so-called blue tsunami that saw Democrats take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections also gave these politicians a mandate to address affordability. And Hakeem Jeffries, the current Speaker-Designate of the House, indicated last week that will be among the priorities for the new Congress come January. “We’re going to relentlessly fight for an affordable America,” Jeffries said in a press conference. “We’re going to work hard to drive down the high cost of groceries and gas and housing.”.

    According to recent reports, but it’s not just BNPL that’s increasingly popular among the highest earning Americans. Block’s study found that four of seven different deferred-payment options were more commonly used by the highest earners, including the option to split a purchase into payments after making it or using an installment proposal from a store, provider or lender.

    It has been revealed that though Block has a dog in the race—it owns Afterpay and Cash App, both of which offer deferred-payment options—the organization contends that their growing popularity isn’t necessarily a sign that people are spending beyond their means. Rather, the company found that 72% of users financed at least one expense in the past year that they technically had the money for, but paying upfront would have felt like a strain, while 47% opted to spread out payments to leave money set aside for savings, investments or other priorities.

    The report reveals how people weigh the trade-offs of the cost of financing versus keeping cash in their accounts.

    Recent findings suggest that “People don’t look at their checking balance and think of it all as money they ⁠can spend,” Juan Hernandez, head of credit and underwriting at Block told Reuters. “​Some of it is already set aside ​for rent, some is for the next bill, and some they want to keep in case something ​goes wrong.”.

    Even so, some of the Block data underscores the strain that many Americans are feeling amid the current affordability crisis that’s seen people struggle to pay for everyday expenses. That’s important as consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of gross domestic product and while Americans have largely weathered the current affordability crisis, one measure of consumer confidence recently fell to the lowest level since 2014.

    The Block study found that people are using deferred-payment methods to finance everyday purchases, like groceries, filling up their tank at the gas station or to pay their utility bills. To cover groceries and other bills, cash advances, earned wage access and/or short-term loans accounted for 58% of these financed transactions.

    And even though a vast majority of consumers—82% of those financing basics and 73% who are financing bills—reported repayment horizons for these expenses within six weeks, that still shows that many people are struggling to keep pace with their day-to-day expenses.

    Such data underscores the findings of a recent survey by Pew Research Center. Among American adults surveyed in August, 27% said they can’t pay some of their monthly bills—or can only afford to make partial payments.

    The so-called blue tsunami that saw Democrats take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections also gave these politicians a mandate to address affordability. And Hakeem Jeffries, the current Speaker-Designate of the House, indicated last week that will be among the priorities for the newly introduced Congress come January.

    “We’re going to relentlessly fight for an affordable America,” Jeffries noted in a press conference. “We’re going to work hard to drive down the high cost of groceries and gas and housing.”.

    It’s that time of year again, when people flood social media with year-end reviews and music lovers start counting down to what may be the most anticipated of them all: Spotify Wrapped. Spotify Wrapped 2026 reveals not just your top five songs (you know, those embarrassing tunes you’ve got on repeat), it also stacks your minutes and musical tastes up against the general public—for better or worse. (In past years, it also revealed listeners’ most-streamed songs, favorite artists, and podcasts.) Last year, some 500 million users shared their stories on social media in the first 24 hours, an overall increase of 41% year over year from 2025. When Does Spotify Wrapped drop? While the company hasn’t officially declared the release date for Spotify Wrapped 2026, the streaming platform’s past history reveals some good clues about when to expect it—and that date is coming up fast. Last year, Spotify Wrapped dropped soon after Thanksgiving, on December 3. In 2024, it came out one day later, on December 4. Before that, in 2023 and 2022, it came out November 29 and 30, respectively, near Thanksgiving weekend. However, since 2021, Spotify Wrapped has released on a Wednesday, often right after Thanksgiving, which this year falls on December 2. A look at online prediction market Kalshi highlights traders giving Spotify Wrapped 2026 only a 21% chance of dropping before December 2, but forecasting an 88% chance before December 3, and a 90% chance before December 4. How can I see Spotify Wrapped once it releases? Spotify listeners can view their personalized recap in Spotify’s mobile app and share results on social media platforms such as Instagram and TikTok. To get the updated app, scan the QR code to download Spotify.

    Latest Update: At $600, the Pixel 10 is this year’s no-brainer Black Friday smartphone deal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better.
    • While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year.
    • So what are you giving up that matters?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better. If you’re in the market for an upgrade, this year’s Black Friday might be one of the final truly good times to buy a upcoming device, and for just $600, last year’s Pixel 10 should be high on your list.

    While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year. From a hardware perspective, nearly everything is either identical or close enough to not particularly matter. Its design and display are all but unchanged, Qi2-ready magnets come on both models, and both devices are built with the same level of battery longevity in mind. And much to the chagrin of many a Pixel die-hard, Tensor G5 and Tensor G6 are practically interchangeable.

    So what are you giving up that matters? When the Pixel 11 arrived, software features made up the bulk of this list, but with last week’s Pixel Drop, a lot of the gaps between these two generations have been closed. Gemini Intelligence with Rambler, app automation, and more are in the process of rolling out to existing Pixel 10 customers, and new features like Create My Widget arrived on the Pixel 10 and 11 at the exact same time. From a software perspective — Google’s bread and butter, in my eyes — the only big sacrifice comes from the year of software support that’s already complete, leaving you with just six instead of seven.

    Sources indicate that realistically, the camera is the one place you’re likely to feel a difference. The Pixel 10 was the first non-Pro device in Google’s Tensor era to ship with a telephoto lens, but it came with some big sacrifices. The main sensor is effectively an A-series lens, and taken together, the entire package might leave something to be desired. It’s far from a bad camera though — I used it as my main shooter through most of its lifecycle — and while the Pixel 11 did get some upgrades here, I think real shutterbugs would be better off looking at Google’s Pro lineup anyway. You’ll also lose out on things like HiLight, though really, are you missing that much?

    In a recent development, what makes this deal so good is really its place in the market, not as a direct comparison to the newer Pixel 11. For $600, Google’s competition is going to have a hard time competing with the value the Pixel 10 delivers. Hell, even Google might find it difficult to compete in the coming months; at full price, $600 is what the Pixel 10a goes for now, a decidedly less-impressive device compared to this model. No, this is a flagship smartphone through and through, and for $600, you’re effectively guaranteeing a reliable, powerful smartphone experience from now until 2032 — hopefully enough time for this whole RAM crisis to finally simmer down a bit.

    Building a modern web API is only half the battle. Ensuring it is secure, resilient, and capable of handling malicious traffic is what separates a hobby project from a production-ready service. When building highly scalable applications, we typically lean on stateless architectures. However, features like token revocation and rate limiting require state.

    In this guide, we will explore the architectural concepts behind building a secure API using FastAPI, Redis, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SlowAPI. We will break down the theory, the tech stack, and the flow of data—without getting bogged down in the code.

    Before diving into the architecture, it is crucial to understand the role each tool plays in our security model:.

    Recent findings suggest that security starts with how you manage your secrets. The first step in our architectural journey is setting up a configuration file and a local environment file.

    Hardcoding secret keys, database URLs, or algorithm types directly into your application is a severe security risk. Instead, we load these from environment variables. The application uses a settings manager to read variables like the Redis host, port, the JWT secret key, the algorithm (typically HS256), and the token expiration time. This ensures that sensitive data stays out of your version control system.

    To handle rate limiting and token tracking, we need a connection to Redis. Because FastAPI is inherently asynchronous, we initialize an asynchronous Redis client.

    Industry observers note that redis acts as the central state-holder for our API. By using Redis, we ensure that even if our API is running on five different servers behind a load balancer, the rate limits and the token blacklists remain globally synchronized.

    Next, we establish the utility functions that handle the cryptographic heavy lifting. This step is divided into two main parts:.

    Here, we initialize the FastAPI application and attach slowapi.

    It has been revealed that slowapi needs a way to identify the client making the request. By default, it uses the client's IP address. We attach the limiter to the application state and register an exception handler. This ensures that if a user breaches the rate limit, the API gracefully returns a "429 Too Many Requests" error instead of crashing.

    According to recent reports, we also set up a dependency that acts as a security guard for our protected routes. This dependency intercepts incoming requests, extracts the token, and decodes it. It then checks Redis to see if the token has been blacklisted (for example, if the user logged out before the token expired). If the token is valid and not blacklisted, the request proceeds; otherwise, a "401 Unauthorized" error is thrown.

    Industry observers note that the login endpoint is where the magic happens. When a user submits their credentials, the API verifies the username and password. In a production scenario, this involves querying a database; in our example, we verify it against a hardcoded credential.

    Once the credentials are validated, the API generates a JWT. To ensure we can invalidate this token later if needed, we store the token in Redis with a time-to-live (TTL) that matches the token's expiration time. Finally, the token is returned to the client, which will store it and send it in the Authorization header of future requests.

    Finally, we create a route that requires both authentication and rate limiting.

    Before the route's logic even executes, two things happen:.

    If the client passes both security checks, they are granted access to the highly secure data provided by the route.

    To validate this system, you would conceptually walk through several test scenarios. First, you test the login flow with correct and incorrect credentials to ensure tokens are only issued to valid users.

    Next, you test the rate limit by rapidly firing requests at the protected route to ensure the "429 Too Many Requests" response triggers. Finally, you test the security guard by trying to access the route with no token, an expired token, and a manually blacklisted token to ensure the API correctly denies access in all scenarios.

    Building a secure API requires layering defenses. By combining FastAPI's speed, Redis's fast state management, JWT's stateless authentication, and slowapi's rate-limiting capabilities, you create a system that is both robust and scalable.

    According to recent reports, while this foundational text explains the core concepts, moving to production requires adding token refresh flows, implementing per-user rate limiting (rather than just IP-based), deploying Redis with high availability, and ensuring your secrets are managed by a secure vault. These practices will ensure your API remains secure as your user base grows.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, just 11 days after his closely watched exit from the tech giant he cofounded—even as he remains mired in controversy. In an announcement this morning, the Nvidia board claimed to be “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia,” following a number of meetings with the newly reinstated CEO. The chairman said the board “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia,” and that his return atop the company is “in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”  There was little mention of the circumstances that led to Huang’s departure, aside from an assurance that the board had conferred with senior government officials and are now “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” The announcement noted that an independent investigation is still underway to probe the fallout from Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and that Huang intended to cooperate. Huang’s reinstatement is not entirely a surprise (though it was apparently a surprise to interim CEO Colette Kress, who was not consulted on the decision, per a Bloomberg report). By the board’s own admission, the decision seems to have been influenced by President Donald Trump, who has remained a steadfast supporter of Huang throughout the debacle. But Trump was more explicit about his role in a CNBC interview today, revealing that he spoke directly to the company’s board. “And I convinced them,” he said. “I made the deal.” Trump also noted, “We have to protect our geniuses.” As Fast Company reported earlier today, Huang’s return underscores his influence as a key player in the AI boom (not to mention his cozy relationship with Trump). Since Huang resigned, there has been a steady drumbeat of concern from the tech community, with prominent figures like Elon Musk and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick arguing that he should be reinstated. At the Newly introduced York Times DealBook summit last week, Musk argued, “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen,” and likened his resignation to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” (Other leaders at the conference also spoke highly of Huang, from Sam Altman to Anduril’s Palmer Luckey.) In a recent appearance, Kalanick drew parallels to his own experience being ousted from Uber and said, “We gotta bring Jensen back.” Y Combinator cofounder Paul Graham boldly asserted, “I’ve never known the tech world to be more unanimous about anything than they are about Jensen Huang.” Despite allegations of multiple inappropriate relationships with his own employees—including a direct report—apparently plenty of Nvidia staffers also expressed solidarity with Huang. A Wired report last week revealed that some employees immediately urged the board to bring Huang back in internal posts. A widely circulated petition to reinstate Huang as CEO drew more than 200,000 signatures, of which more than 10,000 were from current Nvidia employees—about a quarter of the company’s workforce. Musk, Kalanick, and a handful of other CEOs and business leaders signed the petition. It didn’t take long for Huang to plead his own case. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” he said last week, hours before the company’s first earnings call without him. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” He also acknowledged that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia” and had made “serious mistakes” in his personal life. At the time, the board continued to insist that there was no proposal to bring him back. But now that Huang is at the helm again, is it back to business as usual? There are all kinds of questions about what his return could mean for Nvidia, and not just in terms of the serious national security concerns raised by his indiscretions. The board is still conducting an investigation into the events that led to Huang’s exit, but it could be little more than a formality if he has already been reinstated. (Or perhaps the board will find itself in yet another bind when that investigation surfaces new information.)  While the board now claims to be convinced of Huang’s candor, it was quite the opposite just two weeks ago, per a Wired report, when his “lack of candor” and “lying” apparently pushed the board to remove him. As Fast Company previously reported, boards usually have little tolerance for CEOs pursuing romantic relationships with their subordinates (and the stock price often takes a dip following such revelations). Nvidia also has an unusually flat organizational structure, in which Huang has 60 direct reports, an arrangement that seems to have left the company without a succession plan—while making its CEO even more powerful. A New York Times investigation last week raised further concerns over Huang’s leadership at Nvidia, which seems to have created a culture of fear at the company. While many employees remain loyal to Huang—and even seem to revere him—others claim to have experienced ritual humiliation under his rule. More than a dozen former and current employees said Huang frequently used insults and personal attacks to motivate his staff. According to The Times, Huang could be particularly creative with his insults, telling an executive that his mother should have aborted him, and in another instance threatening to rip off an employee’s head and “pee on your brain.”  The report found that Huang’s management style had sparked regular HR complaints—which some employees said weren’t adequately addressed—and that a former HR leader had been fired for calling attention to Huang’s conduct, which he characterized as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” that he had seen in his career. (The former employee threatened to sue but ultimately reached a settlement with Nvidia for more than $1 million, The Times reported.) At the moment, it’s not clear how or whether Nvidia looks to address these complications, along with Huang’s other transgressions. His statement today stops short of introspection or insight into what—if anything—could change upon his return. “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in his statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.” It remains to be seen whether Huang will approach the job any differently. In the meantime, since news of his return broke this morning, Nvidia stock is up over 30%.

    Industry observers note that A Fresh York Times investigation last week raised further concerns over Huang’s leadership at Nvidia, which seems to have created a culture of fear at the company. While many employees remain loyal to Huang—and even seem to revere him—others claim to have experienced ritual humiliation under his rule. More than a dozen former and current employees mentioned Huang frequently used insults and personal attacks to motivate his staff.

    According to The Times, Huang could be particularly creative with his insults, telling an executive that his mother should have aborted him, and in another instance threatening to rip off an employee’s head and “pee on your brain.”.

    The report found that Huang’s management style had sparked regular HR complaints—which some employees noted weren’t adequately addressed—and that a former HR leader had been fired for calling attention to Huang’s conduct, which he characterized as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” that he had seen in his career. (The former employee threatened to sue but ultimately reached a settlement with Nvidia for more than $1 million, The Times reported.).

    At the moment, it’s not clear how or whether Nvidia plans to address these concerns, along with Huang’s other transgressions. His statement today stops short of introspection or insight into what—if anything—could change upon his return.

    “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang noted in his statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

    It has been revealed that it remains to be seen whether Huang will approach the job any differently. In the meantime, since news of his return broke this morning, Nvidia stock is up over 30%.

    Creating polished visual content used to require professional equipment, editing skills and hours of manual work. Generative AI has changed that for photographers, designers, marketers and developers who build creative tools, but the results depend heavily on understanding what these systems actually do. Two techniques sit at the center of most workflows: image-to-image generation, which transforms an existing picture, and image-to-video generation, which adds motion to a still.

    This article explains how both techniques work, which settings control the outcome, how several kinds of tools differ, and how to assemble a workflow with review steps, including a short code example you can run yourself. It also covers rights, authenticity and the limits of the technology. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you plan a production.

    According to recent reports, image-to-image resembles text-to-image, but it starts from your picture instead of pure noise. According to the Hugging Face Diffusers image-to-image guide, the initial image is encoded into latent space and noise is added to it. The model then uses the prompt and the noisy latent to predict and remove that noise, and a decoder converts the result back into an image.

    A single setting, usually called strength or creativity, decides how much of the original remains. In Diffusers, a higher strength gives the model more freedom, and a value of 1.0 means the starting image is largely ignored. Strength is linked to the number of denoising steps: with 50 inference steps and a strength of 0.8, the pipeline adds noise for 40 steps and then denoises for 40.

    According to recent reports, the ranges above are rules of thumb, not guarantees. Models and tools respond differently, so test on your own images. The script below, adapted from the Diffusers documentation, sweeps four strength values on one source image so you can compare them side by side.

    Running this requires a compatible GPU setup and model downloads, and the checkpoint name and defaults can change between library versions, so check the current documentation.

    Recent findings suggest that plain image-to-image can drift from the layout you wanted. Research such as ControlNet adds spatial control to pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, with conditions such as edges, depth, segmentation and human pose. In practice, this is why many tools offer reference images, sketches, masks and pose guides on top of a prompt: they supply structure that a text prompt cannot describe precisely.

    In a recent development, the key advantage is speed of iteration. The main limits are consistency between variations, small details such as hands and text, and the gap between a convincing concept and a usable final asset.

    Sources indicate that the right tool depends on what you need to control and where the output will be used. The table summarizes what each vendor’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

    OpenArt’s own page describes an AI image to image generator that accepts JPEG, PNG, WEBP or HEIC files, offers a creativity slider and an optional reference image, and lets you switch between several models. Its FAQ advises uploading only images you own or have rights to use. Adobe’s Firefly page describes generative editing and video tools and states that outputs include Content Credentials, while saying its own models were trained on licensed and public-domain content. These are vendor statements, so read the current terms for the blueprint you use.

    Image-to-video uses a still as the starting point for an animated scene. Most current systems extend diffusion models across time, so that a whole sequence of frames is denoised together. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequence is that the first frame strongly shapes what follows, so a clean composition and a clear subject make better clips.

    For example, a still of a person walking through a rainy city can be animated with falling rain, reflections and a slow camera move. The motion instruction should describe one clear action and one camera movement rather than a long list.

    Kling’s main site announces Kling 4.0 and describes stable dynamic motion with an audio-visual experience, with image-to-video features and an API platform listed. OpenArt’s Kling 4.0 page describes how the model is offered on that platform. According to that page, videos run from 3 to 30 seconds at 720p to 1080p, you can use up to 10 keyframes and up to 15 references, and you can save a character for reuse. The page does not state pricing or generation quotas for the model. Capabilities depend on the platform that provides access and on the settings available there, so check supported inputs, output limits and cost before planning a production.

    According to recent reports, generated motion needs checking. Warped limbs, drifting faces, flickering textures and unwanted text are common. A quick review script samples frames and reports basic file properties:.

    Industry observers note that this process reduces the effort of exploring concepts and makes it easier to test several versions of an advertisement before choosing a direction. It does not remove the need for human review.

    They can be, with different priorities. Photographers can explore creative treatments, mood boards and alternative backgrounds without replacing traditional photography. Marketers can develop campaign concepts, create variations of social graphics and test promotional videos. In both cases the value comes from supporting a clear creative objective rather than adopting a tool because it is new.

    It depends on the tool, the strategy and the rights you hold in the inputs. Read the current terms and keep records of your sources.

    Image-to-image and image-to-video tools give creators a faster way to explore ideas, but they work best when you understand their controls. Strength settings decide how much of the original survives, conditioning methods preserve structure, and the starting frame shapes video. Compare hosted platforms, vendor apps and open-source libraries against your needs, build review and provenance into the workflow, and treat the output as a draft that a person checks before it ships.

Just pop off the side shell (it’s held in by simple plastic clips), unscrew the SSD cover, slide in the M2 SSD, then close it all up. Boom, double the storage for just a few minutes’ work! And hey, if you ever get rid of the PS5 or just want to move the drive to another machine, lots of laptops and other similar larger electronics use M2 SSDs these days, so this could be a great longer-term investment.

    In a recent development, if you want to double that storage, the 2TB model is down to $293.99, making it $52 off the normal price. RAM and storage prices are at an all-time high right now (and have been for months), making this a deal you’re not going to find very often. Considering regular prices aren’t expected to drop any time soon (think years, not months), this is probably your best bet for doubling your PS5’s storage any time in the near future.

    The Google Search homepage is embracing Gemini in a big way, with a newly introduced sidebar redesign that puts your chat history just a click away.

    In a recent development, google’s AI ambitions have been anything but subtle in their integration with Search, but Gemini and Search have had some clear separations. But, with its latest enhancement, Google is very much intertwining the two.

    Confirmed by Google’s Robby Stein on Twitter/X, Google is now rolling out a desktop homepage revamp that gives Gemini near-top billing.

    At first glance, you’ve got the typical blank canvas with a Google logo and Search bar at the center, but the fresh changes start with Gemini-powered shortcuts underneath for actions such as creating images, analyzing files, and “brainstorming” with Gemini.

    People are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done – and in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.

    It has been revealed that the upcoming Google Search homepage is now rolling out globally, Stein states, though we’re not seeing it live just yet on our devices. Sound off in the comments if you’re seeing the new look and whether or not you like this functionality.

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google introduced 3D emoji on Pixel this year, and has just detailed the minimum specifications required to get them on your Android phone.
    • Enhancement: Google replied on Reddit to “clear up some confusion” about the Help Center page.
    • Noto 3D emoji, with its high-resolution bitmap approach, uses less than 220 MB of storage versus the previous 2D vector font that comes in at around 3 MB.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google introduced 3D emoji on Pixel this year, and has just detailed the minimum specifications required to get them on your Android phone.

    Enhancement: Google replied on Reddit to “clear up some confusion” about the Help Center page. The listed storage and RAM requirements refer to the “automatic background download via Google Play services on eligible Android 17 devices that didn’t ship with the 3D font preinstalled.” The support article did not make that distinction.

    Noto 3D emoji, with its high-resolution bitmap approach, uses less than 220 MB of storage versus the previous 2D vector font that comes in at around 3 MB.

    During installation, Google Play services temporarily needs a bit of extra headroom to copy the file into place before immediately clearing its download cache.

    Meanwhile, Google said RAM usage is “minimal & transient” as “Android doesn’t load the 3D emoji font file into RAM.” The support page listed 6 GB as a “cutoff to ensure lower-memory devices stay on the lightweight ~3 MB 2D vector font.”.

    Noto 3D emoji goes from vector-based 2D emoji to a high-resolution bitmap font. This results in “high-resolution designs” for emoji “with more texture and dimension to characters and icons.” Google has an FAQ section about why the latest emoji might look low resolution:.

    Sources indicate that vector vs. bitmap rendering: Older Android emoji used 2D vector graphics, which scale infinitely to any size without losing resolution. The 3D emoji are bitmap graphics, which are pre-rendered pixel-based images. When these images are scaled up by an app or zoomed in, the pixels stretch, which can cause a softer or lower-resolution appearance.

    The Google support article published this week lists the minimum specs your Android device must have to get 3D emoji:.

    Recent findings suggest that the last two bullet points are rather surprising. In fact, Google even lists instructions for checking how much memory and storage your device has:.

    In terms of availability, Google notes a supported device will “automatically download the 3D emoji when it’s on Wi-Fi and charging.”.

    At this time, there isn’t a way to force download the emoji.

    Google confirmed 3D emoji in May, with the upcoming design shipping on the Pixel 11 in August. It has since arrived on older Pixel devices.

    In terms of OEM availability, Google explicitly notes “Samsung devices use a proprietary emoji font and do not receive the 3D font upgrade.” Additionally:.

    This is also true for third-party messaging apps, such as WhatsApp, who use their own emoji fonts rather than relying on your device’s system font.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, corsair's AIR 5400 RS-R midtower PC case is down to its lowest price ever, with a 31% discount bringing the price down to $169.99. The case normally retails for nearly $250, and outside of a short sale last month, we haven't seen it drop below $200. In addition, with a wrap-around glass side panel and triple-chamber design, the case comes with three Corsair RS-R 120mm PWM ARGB fans, which normally run $60 on their own.

    According to recent reports, typical of these multi-chamber case designs, the AIR 5400 RS-R supports most hardware you can throw at it. You can use anything from a mini ITX motherboard to an E-ATX board, and it has mounting points for up to two 360mm radiators, plus an additional 120mm mounting point. The 360mm worth of mounting space on the bottom of the case is occupied by the pre-installed fans and an airflow shroud.

    Additionally, the case is compatible with rear-connector motherboards from Asus, MSI, and Gigabyte, so you can have a cable-free front chamber. The case doesn't have a vertical GPU mount, but there's ample room for even larger graphics cards, with a maximum length of 430 mm supported. Like most multi-chamber cases, this one is primarily designed around liquid cooling. However, you have a generous 180mm of CPU cooler clearance if you decide to go with an air cooler.

    Industry observers note that the Corsair AIR 5400 RS-R is a midtower PC case with three Corsair RS-R 120mm ARGB fans pre-installed. It supports up to E-ATX motherboards, as well as rear-connector boards from MSI, Asus, and Gigabyte.

    Sources indicate that the Corsair AIR 1500 RS-R is loaded with enough features to justify its $250 list price, let alone its current sale price of $170. In addition to wide cooling and GPU compatibility, along with rear-connector motherboard support, the case comes with a built-in anti-sag arm to support your GPU, the height of which you can adjust depending on your GPU. Be warned, however, that the final fan on especially long GPUs may hit the support. Thankfully, you can remove it.

    Corsair includes its RapidRoute 2.0 mounting system, giving you a pegboard-style motherboard tray that provides mounting points virtually anywhere for cable management. Cable managing multi-chamber cases is much easier than a traditional tower, as well, with ample room behind the motherboard tray to hide your cable mess.

    Around the front, the curved-glass side panel highlights off the internals of your rig from the side and front. To get inside, the curved panel splits apart like French doors, so you can service your machine without juggling a few different pieces of tempered glass. The rear side panel is on a hinge for easy access, as well.

    It has been revealed that the one major downside with this chassis is that it doesn't come with any front panel USB-A ports. Instead, you get three USB-C ports, split between two USB 3.2 Gen 1 ports and a single Gen 2 port, alongside a 3.5mm headphone/microphone combo jack. Given that most motherboards have one or maybe two USB-C ports, extra front panel connectors are always nice to have. However, even a single USB-A would go a long way.
